In the final stretch before graduation, the most common subject on campus was no longer youth, but destination.

Some people already knew which work unit they were joining. Some were still searching. Some were excited about the future; others were anxious. Topics that had once filled dormitory conversations late into the night slowly turned into salary, city, job title, and who had received news first.
The identity of student had lasted for many years. Only when it was about to disappear did people realize how simple it had made life.

If an exam went badly, there might be another chance. If living expenses ran short, one could find ways to save. When winter or summer break arrived, there was always somewhere to return to. Once school ended, however, life would no longer be divided into semesters. Work did not come with a “next term” in which to start over. Some mistakes were simply mistakes.
Zhang Yuansheng looked forward to that change and remained wary of it at the same time.

He wanted to work, and he wanted to earn money in his own right. A young man in his twenties could not remain content forever with taking money from home. Yet he had little experience of what real work would be like. He had watched his father’s generation “go to work” for years; when his own turn came, he still felt as though he were standing before another door.
In 1995, he formally entered the workforce.
His work unit was Oilfield Construction Company No. 3.

The words “oilfield construction” were concrete. They were nothing like the abstract future discussed on campus. Projects, sites, schedules, materials, equipment, and people formed an order completely different from the classroom.

On his first day entering the unit as an employee, traces of the student were still on him. The way he spoke, understood rules, and looked at supervisors and colleagues all had to be learned again. University could teach a person knowledge, but rarely how to get one thing completed among dozens of adults with different personalities.
Work quickly began sanding away the unrealistic parts.

Some things cannot be done well simply because you understand the theory. When a task is handed to you, the site does not become easier because you have just graduated. Other people will not patiently explain everything every day. You have to watch, ask, remember, and after making a mistake, learn as quickly as possible.
Zhang Yuansheng was not the kind of young employee who needed everyone to remember him on the first day.
He was more like earth being compacted little by little. At first it did not draw attention, but when something landed on him, he tried to carry it.
That way of working would follow him through almost his entire career.

Decades later, in a flooring company in Calgary, when warehouse inventory failed to match, rolls could not be found, or receiving and shipping did not line up, his instinct would still be the same: where is the problem, and how can we keep it from happening again? What would later become Warehouse OS was, at the beginning, simply that habit pushed into a computer.
But in 1995 he knew none of that.

Computers were still far from becoming an invisible part of ordinary life, and artificial intelligence belonged more to science fiction. A young man just starting work thought about this month’s pay, whether he could establish himself, how colleagues saw him, and whether life would now extend along a fixed path.
In those years, entering a stable work unit often meant that the broad frame of a life had already been built.

Work, marriage, children, an allocated apartment or a home purchase, years of seniority accumulated slowly. That was roughly how the generation before him had lived, and how many people around him expected to live.
Zhang Yuansheng did not reject that kind of stability.

In fact, for a long time he worked seriously to build exactly such a life. An ordinary person does not need to wrestle with fate every day. Stable work, a complete family, healthy parents, children growing up—these are already large things.
But young people do not know the most interesting part of life: a route that appears chosen does not promise to remain straight.
Once he began working, he truly entered the adult world.

Money acquired its own weight. So did time. Being late was no longer something that ended with a teacher’s criticism. Responsibility could not simply be pushed to the next class. More importantly, relationships were no longer simplified by the natural label of “classmate.”

A colleague could become a friend, or remain only a colleague forever. A supervisor’s sentence might carry another meaning beneath it. A young person had to learn slowly when to insist, when to stay quiet, and when finishing the work mattered more than explaining himself.
There was no textbook for any of that.
Zhang Yuansheng learned it little by little.

After work, he was still like any other man in his twenties, with his own lightness and expectations. The future felt long. His parents were not yet old. He had not really understood what the word “middle age” would one day mean.
Love, marriage, and family were still ahead.
And farther away there was a country he would not seriously consider at the time—Canada.

If someone had told him in 1995: eight years from now you will leave here and go to North America to look for work again; twenty-eight years from now you will manage a warehouse by day and clean offices at night; thirty years from now you will sit at a computer with an artificial intelligence, building websites, writing software, and preparing to turn your own life into a novel—
he probably would have laughed.
Because it would not have sounded like a plan.
It would have sounded ridiculous.
But life never hands a person the complete script in advance.
It gives only the next page.
In 1995, the page Zhang Yuansheng received was simple:
Go to work.
He took the page and went.
